intro.overview: This is your Unit 3 Engagement Packet for Module 4. Over the last two units you audited Alamo Industries across its two very different environments: the Windows corporate office (Lab 4.1) and the Linux plant floor (Lab 4.2). Now you compile one client-facing Engagement Packet for Alamo, comparing credential security across the two environments and recommending what to fix first, ahead of their CMMC Level 2 assessment. It is addressed to Elena Vasquez, Alamo’s IT Manager, with Bobby Alamo III, the CEO, as executive sponsor.
objectives: Compile a professional security assessment report using work from Labs 4.1 and 4.2
Compare Windows NTLM and Linux SHA-512 password security architectures
Write an executive summary for non-technical stakeholders
Document professional reflection on the engagement

clientContext.description: A single client, Alamo Industries (San Antonio aerospace and defense, pursuing CMMC Level 2), assessed across two internal environments: the Windows corporate office (NTLM) and the Linux plant floor (SHA-512). Don’t build this from a blank page. Download the pre-formatted NEXUS template (cover, section headings, and auto-generating Table of Contents already set up): EP_M4_Password_Audit.docx. Full instructions are on the Engagement Packet Guide.

callouts.title: Minimum Requirements
callouts.body: Your Engagement Packet must include: Part I (Timesheet, Runbook, Analyst Reflection) and Part II (Cover, Executive Summary, Methodology, Findings, Risk Analysis, Recommendations, Appendix), at least 20 qualifying screenshots from Lab 4.1, Lab 4.2 and EP 4, your abc123 visible in every one, and a minimum of 10 references. RFCs, NIST documents, CVE entries, and man pages all count. Your textbook does NOT count. Use it to find primary sources, then cite those. See the Citations page.

callouts.title: Deadline Tip
callouts.text: Submit at least 10 minutes before the deadline, even if it’s not perfect. Submissions are unlimited. You can keep uploading better versions until time runs out. A 70 beats a zero every time.

content.whatYoureDoing: Downloading the Engagement Packet template, opening it in desktop Word, and setting the two document properties that identify it as yours. Five minutes, before you write a word.
content.whyItMatters: Document mechanics were the single largest avoidable point loss last term, and none of it had anything to do with security knowledge. Nearly all of it traces back to a document set up wrong on day one and never recovered. Do this first and it stays done.

steps.text: Download the template: EP_M4_Password_Audit.docx. Save it somewhere you will find it again.

Open it in desktop Microsoft Word, not Word for the web, not Google Docs, not Preview. Those cannot create the captions, cross-references and citation fields this packet is graded on. Maximize the window so the ribbon shows labels instead of bare icons.

Turn on the Navigation Pane. Windows: View > Navigation Pane. Mac: View > Sidebar > Navigation. Leave it open for the whole engagement. It is how you catch a broken heading before it reaches the Table of Contents.

Set the Author property. Windows: File > Info, the Author box on the right. Mac: File > Properties… > Summary. Word appends your abc123 to the existing author rather than replacing it. That is expected. Leave it.

Set the abc123 custom property. Windows: File > Info > Properties > Advanced Properties > Custom. Mac: File > Properties… > Custom. It has to match the abc123 hostname visible in your screenshots. Together they are how this packet is tied to the machine that produced its evidence.
Fill in the cover page by hand. Type your name in the Analyst / Student cell and your abc123 in the abc123 (VM ID) cell. Nothing on the cover fills itself in from the document properties.
Save the file now, and keep saving as you go.

content.title: Four Mechanics, Every Time
content.body:
Word owns your numbering, not you. Caption every figure with References > Insert Caption. Point at a figure with References > Cross-reference, set to ‘Only label and number’. Add every source with References > Insert Citation > Add New Source. Tick Show All Bibliography Fields first or you cannot enter a URL. Build the reference list with References > Bibliography; the style is already set to APA. Never type a figure number or a reference by hand.

If you have forgotten how any of these work, EP 1, Checkpoint 5 walks all four of them step by step.

content.whatYoureDoing: The foundation of your Engagement Packet: setting up the document and importing your work from Labs 4.1 and 4.2. This engagement compares one client across two environments, Alamo’s corporate Windows domain and its Linux plant floor, in a single client-facing packet.
content.whyItMatters: Professional security reports follow consistent structures. This packet goes to Alamo, so your job is a complete, well-organized report that makes the gap between the two environments clear and tells Elena what to fix first.

content.title: Include in Part I (Internal Packet)
items:
A. Timesheet (5%)
  • Hours per unit: Lab 4.1 (internal training), Lab 4.2 (internal training), EP 4 (client billable to Alamo Industries)
  • Date, specific activity name, and hours per line entry (no “did lab” entries)
  • Internal vs. client-billable split clearly indicated, with an internal-training subtotal and a separate client-billable subtotal
  • Justification narrative for any unusual entries (very high or very low hours on a task)
  • Total hours at the bottom

B. Runbook (20%)
  • One man-page-style entry per tool used across Lab 4.1, Lab 4.2 and EP 4 (John the Ripper, Hashcat, etc.)
  • For each tool: name and purpose, switches used (with one-line explanations), switches not used but worth knowing
  • How you used the tool on the engagement (the actual command, including hash mode and attack mode)
  • What output came back (with screenshot reference, including cracked passwords or session statistics)
  • What you did with the result (how it fed into your platform comparison or Findings)
  • Bar: a colleague picking this up in 3 months should be able to reproduce your engagement
  • Adding entries and placing screenshots: follow Adding a Runbook Entry in the Engagement Packet Guide, the same steps you used in EP 1

C. Analyst Reflection (15%)
  • Timesheet Self-Audit. Was there a task or section that took disproportionately long? Describe what made it slow (a hash mode that wouldn’t crack, attack mode selection, troubleshooting a Hashcat error) and what you’d do differently next time. Then total your hours: if Maya Rodriguez reviewed your timesheet alongside this deliverable, what conclusion would she draw about your efficiency?
  • Professional Reflection. What worked on this engagement? What didn’t? If you ran this password security assessment for Alamo again next semester with what you know now, what would you do differently? Be specific: “I’d benchmark rules-based attacks before brute force” is more useful than “I’d be more organized.”
  • AI Methodology Reflection. Where AI helped you on this engagement, and how you validated what it told you. Strong answers describe specific moments of help and the verification step that followed (e.g., “I asked Claude to explain Hashcat mask syntax; I confirmed against the Hashcat documentation before writing my finding.”). “I didn’t use AI on this engagement (N/A)” is acceptable if true, but don’t claim N/A if your runbook is full of AI-generated explanations.
  • No word floor. No required structure. Honest reflection earns credit; filler doesn’t.

content.title: Include in Part II (Client Deliverable)
items:
Executive Summary (12%)
  • One page maximum. Client-facing and board-readable: no first person, no raw hashes, no jargon
  • Overall risk posture across both environments in one or two sentences
  • Count of findings by severity (e.g., “2 Critical, 3 High”)
  • The headline: corporate versus plant-floor hygiene, and which is worse
  • Top two or three recommendations with business framing (CMMC, DoD exposure)

Methodology (7%)
  • 3 to 4 paragraph narrative of your engagement approach across both environments
  • Phases of the engagement (e.g., hash extraction → identification → attack mode selection → cracking → cross-platform analysis)
  • Scope and limitations: what was in scope, what was not
  • Tools used at a high level (per-flag detail belongs in your Runbook, not here)
  • Written for the client, not for security peers; this is client-facing

Findings (22%)
  • Number each finding sequentially (Finding 1, Finding 2, ...)
  • Descriptive title (e.g., “Domain Administrators Using Easily-Cracked Passwords”)
  • Severity rating (Critical / High / Medium / Low / Informational)
  • Affected platform (Windows NTLM / Linux SHA-512) and environment (Corporate / Plant)
  • Description, including hash type, crack time, and attack method that succeeded
  • Evidence: reference to your screenshot(s) or session output (e.g., “See Figure 4 in Appendix”)
  • Impact statement in business terms (lateral movement risk, credential reuse, regulatory exposure)
  • Per-finding recommendation summary (one line; full remediation lives in Recommendations)
  • Order findings by severity, highest first
  • After your last numbered finding, add a Platform Comparison subheading inside Findings: your speed table and your answers to the four analysis questions from Checkpoint 3. It is part of Findings, not a separate section.

Risk Analysis (11%)
  • Per-finding likelihood × impact analysis
  • Business context per environment: the corporate office versus the plant floor, both under Alamo’s CMMC obligations (shared accounts, legacy OT systems, DoD exposure)
  • Answer “so what?” for each finding: why does this matter to each business
  • Differentiated reasoning per finding (avoid uniform “high risk” labels with no logic)
  • Reference an authoritative risk framework where helpful (NIST SP 800-63B Digital Identity Guidelines, CIS Controls)

Recommendations (8%)
  • Prioritized: Monday-morning fixes (low effort, immediate impact) vs. next-quarter budget items (higher effort, strategic)
  • Each recommendation specific: what to do, what effort required, what priority window
  • Differentiated by environment (some recs apply only to the corporate Windows environment, others to the plant-floor Linux environment)
  • Aligned with findings (each recommendation maps to one or more findings)
  • Where applicable, indicate which control framework the recommendation aligns with (NIST SP 800-63B, CIS Controls v8, NIST CSF)

content.whatYoureDoing: The core analytical work of your report: comparing Windows NTLM and Linux SHA-512 password security architectures using your own cracking data.
content.whyItMatters: This is THE teaching moment of Module 4. You have empirical evidence showing that the same password cracks thousands of times faster on Windows than Linux. The difference isn’t password complexity. It’s defensive architecture. This is why security professionals argue about platform choices.

content.title: Where This Goes in Your Report
content.body: The Platform Comparison goes inside your Findings section in Part II, as its own subheading after your last numbered finding. Numbered findings first (Finding 1, Finding 2, ..., highest severity first), then the comparison: the speed table built from your own numbers, the calculated difference (“NTLM cracked roughly X times faster”), and your answers to the four questions below. Risk Analysis and Recommendations follow, as usual.

steps.text: Create a speed comparison table using your actual data. This is the same comparison you built in Lab 4.2, Checkpoint 4; bring that table into your Findings here rather than starting a new one:
Answer these four analysis questions in your report:
substeps: Why did NTLM hashes crack faster than SHA-512?
What defensive mechanisms does Linux use that Windows NTLM lacks?
Which environment, the corporate office or the plant floor, faces greater credential risk? Why?
What would you recommend each environment prioritize?

steps.text: Explain the technical reasons for speed differences:
substeps: NTLM: Single-pass MD4, no salt, no iterations
SHA-512: Salted, 5000+ rounds of key derivation

content.text: Why does Windows still use NTLM? Research backward compatibility requirements and Active Directory authentication. Microsoft has been trying to deprecate NTLM for over a decade. Why is it still everywhere?

items.label: Generic comparisons
items.text: Use YOUR actual speed data (John’s c/s, Hashcat’s H/s), not hypotheticals.

items.label: Missing the “why”
items.text: Don’t just say “SHA-512 is slower.” Explain salting and key stretching.

items.label: Forgetting business context
items.text: Connect technical findings to each environment’s situation.

content.body: Chapter 15’s “Password Attacks” section covers brute force, dictionary attacks, and rainbow tables: the techniques you applied hands-on in Labs 4.1 and 4.2. Your platform comparison analysis translates Chapter 15’s theory into observed results: why NTLM without salting falls to rainbow tables while SHA-512 with per-user salts demands targeted, slower attacks.

content.whatYoureDoing: Tailored, prioritized remediation recommendations for Alamo’s corporate and plant-floor environments, based on your findings and each environment’s risk context.
content.whyItMatters: Security findings without actionable recommendations are just bad news. Clients hire consultants for solutions, not just problems. Your recommendations need to be specific, prioritized, and consider each environment’s unique constraints and objectives.

content.text: What is credential stuffing and how does it differ from password spraying? Research how attackers use breached credential databases.

content.title: IT Manager, Alamo Industries
content.quote: The corporate domain runs on NTLM and I can push a policy to force better passwords tomorrow. The plant floor is the hard part: shared accounts, old service accounts, and Frank fighting every change. I need your recommendations to separate the two.

content.title: CEO, Alamo Industries
content.quote: We’re working toward CMMC certification for our DoD contracts. I need documentation showing we’re addressing credential security. Elena keeps telling me the shared supervisor account is a problem. Frank keeps blocking changes. Give me evidence to settle this.

steps.text: Corporate (Windows/NTLM) Recommendations:
substeps: Consider Active Directory migration path away from NTLM
Implement password complexity AND length requirements
Deploy MFA for all privileged accounts immediately
Establish password rotation policy with breach monitoring

steps.text: Plant floor (Linux/SHA-512) Recommendations:
substeps: Eliminate shared supervisor account (CMMC requirement)
Implement individual accountability for all access
Strengthen already-good SHA-512 implementation
Document controls for CMMC evidence package

steps.text: Prioritize each recommendation using High / Medium / Low based on three factors:
substeps: Risk severity: what happens if we don’t fix it?
Implementation complexity: how hard is this?
Business impact: does this affect operations?

content.whatYoureDoing: Walking the finished packet end to end, refreshing everything Word computes for you, and stripping out everything that was only ever scaffolding. Ten minutes.
content.whyItMatters: Every deduction in this category is avoidable and none of it is about security. A packet that goes out with placeholder text still in it, a Table of Contents that describes an earlier draft, or a figure number that points at the wrong picture tells the client nobody read the document before sending it. They will wonder what else nobody checked.

steps.text: Refresh every field. Windows: Ctrl+A then F9. Mac: ⌘A then F9. If nothing happens, your function keys are set to media controls; hold Fn as well, or use the Fn Lock key.
Rebuild the Table of Contents. Right-click it and choose Update Field > Update entire table. Not ‘page numbers only’. That will not pick up sections you added or removed.

Read the Navigation Pane top to bottom. No blank entries. No figure captions. Only real sections. A blank entry means an empty paragraph is carrying a heading style. Click in it and apply Home > Styles > Normal. A caption in the list means it was formatted by hand instead of with Insert Caption.
Compare the Table of Contents against the Navigation Pane. They read from the same source, so they should match exactly. If they disagree, you did not update the entire table.

Click every figure number and every reference to a figure. A real field shades gray when your cursor enters it; typed text does nothing. Anything that does not shade gray was typed by hand and will be wrong the moment something moves. Replace it with References > Insert Caption or References > Cross-reference.

Rebuild the reference list. Click it and press F9, or run References > Bibliography again. Count the entries: you need ten besides the textbook, and every one of them has to appear at least once in the body of the packet. A source that sits in the list and is never cited does not count.

Replace or delete EVERY item in square brackets. Not most of them: all of them. The template ships with roughly 84 bracketed slots: some are places your content goes, some are prompts telling you what belongs there, and both are scaffolding that must be gone before you submit. Search for the bracket character itself. Windows: Ctrl+F. Mac: ⌘F. Type a single [ and step through every hit. Replace it with your own work, or delete the line entirely if that section does not apply. Then search again and confirm you get zero results. The runbook skeleton and the finding card are where they hide.

Check your document properties survived. Windows: File > Info. Mac: File > Properties…. Your abc123 in the Author field and in the abc123 custom property, matching the abc123 hostname visible in your screenshots.
Look at every screenshot at full size. Legible, cropped to what matters, abc123 visible in the prompt. A screenshot nobody can read is evidence of nothing.
Save as .docx and submit that. Word format only, not PDF, not Pages, not Google Docs. The file’s metadata is part of how submissions are verified, and exporting to another format destroys it.

Open what you submitted. Right after you upload, open your submission in Canvas and click the file to preview it. Make sure it’s your finished Engagement Packet for this lab, not the assignment sheet, not the blank template, and not a previous lab’s packet. Canvas’s preview sometimes shows Table of Contents page numbers that don’t match your file. That is the preview, not your document, and packets are graded in Word.

content.title: Check the File You Submitted
content.body: Open your submission in Canvas before the due date and confirm it’s the right file: your finished Engagement Packet for this lab. If you upload the wrong file (the assignment sheet, the blank template, or a previous lab’s packet), that is what gets graded. You won’t be given a chance to fix it after the due date.

content.title: Leftover Brackets Cost You 10%
content.body: −10%, flat, triggered by a single surviving bracket. Not per-item: one is the same as forty, because the failure is the same failure: nobody read the document before sending it. A packet that reaches the client still saying [what this tool/step accomplishes and why] or [Title of your highest-severity finding] is marked accordingly. It is also the most preventable deduction on the list. Search for [ and confirm zero results before you submit.

items: Updating ‘page numbers only’ instead of the entire table. The page numbers will be right and the section list will describe a document you no longer have.
